The work is removal-only and verbatim for catalog text, uses guarded SQL, keeps a penalty rather than a hard filter, reverts the single-intent chain hook when the evidence turned against it, reports unwired fan-in instead of inventing it, and marks degraded decompositions. The packet is unusually candid about its limits. The main problems are in three areas. First, the step-8a data-kind detector is a brittle regex with at least one concrete cross-domain false positive. Worse, it is applied to whatever query string reaches `_calculate_score`: in fork/join branches that string is the LLM's `task_spec`, whose own worked example would not trigger detection, so the fix likely does not cover the external user's DIA-NN case. Second, the catalog passes edit up to ~22% of rows with no row-level audit trail. Their acceptance rule is agreement between two LLMs that see near-identical prompts, and the 'applied only to BioMate-authored rows' restriction is not in the code. Third, the evaluation does not support several claims. The current arm G is worse than baseline on loose target (10/12 vs 12/12) and on controls (25/28 vs 27/28); the penalty was tuned on the test row; and the catalog-wide executability change was measured by a single 20×2 arm. There are also a few concrete code defects: substring (not word-bounded) phrase removal, a long GET query string that can silently disable card lookups, intent/result index alignment in the DAG path, and per-branch parameters dropped when routed paths are reused. Neither the deploy nor the core designs should be rolled back wholesale.
